title: YOUR ANOINTING DOES NOT MAKE YOU IMMUNE TO SEXUAL TEMPTATION
paragraphs: YOUR ANOINTING DOES NOT MAKE YOU IMMUNE TO SEXUAL TEMPTATION
You can love God, carry a calling, know Scripture, feel the presence of the Holy Spirit—and still destroy something precious if you start believing temptation cannot destroy you.
There is a dangerous moment in the life of a believer that rarely looks dangerous when it begins.
It is the moment you start trusting yesterday’s victories more than today’s dependence on Jesus.
You have prayed.
You have worshiped.
Maybe you have preached.

Maybe people come to you for spiritual advice. Maybe you lead a ministry, serve faithfully in church, post Scripture online, counsel struggling believers, or have watched God use your testimony to bring somebody else back from the edge.
And somewhere inside you, almost imperceptibly, a thought can begin growing:
“I would never do that.”
That sentence should frighten us more than temptation itself.
Because Scripture does not say, “Let anyone who thinks that he stands celebrate how strong he has become.”
It says:
“Therefore let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall.”
—1 Corinthians 10:12
The Greek is painfully direct:
ὁ δοκῶν ἑστάναι βλεπέτω μὴ πέσῃ
ho dokōn hestanai blepetō mē pesē
The word βλεπέτω — blepetō carries the force of “let him watch,” “let him pay attention,” “let him beware.”
Paul is speaking to believers.
People inside the covenant community.
People surrounded by spiritual privilege.
And his warning is essentially this:
Watch yourself.
Not because Christ is weak.
Because you are not Christ.
You can be genuinely used by God and still be genuinely vulnerable to temptation.
That truth may offend the part of us that wants spiritual maturity to mean spiritual invulnerability.
But Scripture refuses to flatter us.
David was not an atheist when he saw Bathsheba.
Samson was not without divine calling when his desires repeatedly pulled him toward destruction.
Peter was not an unbeliever when his confidence collapsed under pressure.
The Bible is brutally honest about its heroes because God never needed sanitized people to prove the power of grace.
And perhaps somebody reading this needs that honesty tonight.
Because you love Jesus.
But there is a battle you have not told anybody about.
There is a name you keep thinking about.
A conversation you know has become too intimate.
A screen you keep returning to after everybody is asleep.
A marriage boundary you have started mentally renegotiating.
Pornography you promised God would be “the last time.”
Messages you delete.
Fantasies you entertain because you tell yourself thoughts are harmless.
A coworker whose attention feels increasingly good.
An old relationship you should never have reopened.
Or perhaps nothing outward has happened yet.
That word matters.
Yet.
Because almost nobody wakes up one morning intending to destroy their marriage, fracture their family, wound their children, compromise their witness, and spend years trying to rebuild trust.
Sexual sin usually begins much quieter than the explosion it eventually causes.
A glance becomes permission.
Permission becomes imagination.
Imagination becomes anticipation.
Anticipation becomes secrecy.
Secrecy becomes opportunity.
And opportunity eventually asks you to become the person you once swore you would never become.
James describes the progression with terrifying precision:
“But each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire. Then desire when it has conceived gives birth to sin; and sin when it is full-grown brings forth death.”
The Greek word translated “desire” is ἐπιθυμία — epithymia.
Desire.
Craving.
Longing.

The problem is not that human beings experience desire. God created sexuality. Within His design, sexual intimacy is not dirty or shameful. Scripture presents marriage and marital intimacy with dignity.
The danger begins when desire stops submitting to God.
When desire starts saying:
“I deserve this.”
“Nobody will know.”
“My marriage is difficult.”
“I’m lonely.”
“I’m stressed.”
“My spouse doesn’t understand me.”
“It’s only pornography.”
“We’re only talking.”
“I can stop whenever I want.”
“God knows my heart.”
Yes.
God does know your heart.
That is precisely why Scripture tells us to guard it.
Sexual temptation does not check your ministry résumé before knocking.
It does not care how many Bible verses you know.
It does not become intimidated because people call you “anointed.”
And spiritual experiences do not cancel biological desire, emotional loneliness, unresolved wounds, pride, opportunity, or the deceitfulness of sin.
Look at David.
The tragedy of 2 Samuel 11 begins with an almost haunting sentence:
“In the spring of the year, the time when kings go out to battle, David sent Joab…”
David sent somebody else.
Then one evening he rose from his couch.
He walked on the roof.
He saw a woman bathing.
And Scripture tells us she was beautiful.
David inquired about her.
Someone answered:
“Is not this Bathsheba, the daughter of Eliam, the wife of Uriah the Hittite?”
That should have ended everything.
The wife of Uriah.
There was the boundary.
There was the warning.
There was the exit.
But David crossed it.
This was David.
The shepherd who faced Goliath.
The songwriter whose words would comfort generations.
The king God had raised up.
The man who had experienced extraordinary deliverance.
None of it made him immune.
And notice something uncomfortable:
David did not lose his knowledge of God before he sinned.
He ignored what he knew.
That is one of the frightening realities of temptation.
Sometimes the distance between knowing truth and obeying truth is one private decision.
David took Bathsheba.
She became pregnant.
Then the sin that promised pleasure demanded protection.
So deception followed.
Then manipulation.
Then Uriah’s death.
Then concealment.
Sexual sin rarely remains alone.
It recruits lies.
It recruits secrecy.
It recruits rationalization.
It recruits hypocrisy.
It recruits other sins to protect itself.
And eventually Nathan stood before the king.
David could command armies.
He could silence critics.
He could hide evidence from people.
But he could not hide from God.
Nathan said:
“You are the man!”
And suddenly the king was no longer looking at somebody else’s scandal.
He was looking at himself.
Maybe that is where this article finds you.
Not standing over someone else’s failure.
Standing in front of your own reflection.
Conviction can be mercy.
The God exposing the darkness is the same God calling you toward the Light.
David’s story did not end with the sentence, “You are the man.”
After Nathan confronted him, David said:
“I have sinned against the LORD.”
No public-relations strategy.
No blaming Bathsheba.
No “but you don’t understand what I was going through.”
No pretending his calling canceled his accountability.
“I have sinned.”
And Psalm 51 allows us to hear the brokenness of his repentance:
“Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me.”
The Hebrew is unforgettable:
לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא־לִי אֱלֹהִים
Lev tahor bera-li Elohim.
“Create for me a clean heart, O God.”
David did not merely ask God to repair his reputation.
He wanted God to deal with his heart.
There is a difference between being sorry you were exposed and grieving because you sinned against God.
There is a difference between damage control and repentance.
Repentance does not ask only:
“How can I keep people from finding out?”
Repentance asks:
“How did I allow my heart to wander this far from the God who loves me?”
And if you have already fallen sexually, hear this carefully:
Your sin is serious.
But Jesus Christ is greater than your sin.
That does not make consequences imaginary.

Forgiveness does not automatically restore shattered trust overnight. Repentance may require confession, accountability, radical boundaries, counseling, patience, and accepting consequences you desperately wish you could erase.
Grace is not God pretending sin did not matter.
Grace is why sinners who could never cleanse themselves can be washed through Christ.
This is where the Gospel becomes more than a religious slogan.
Jesus did not come because respectable people needed polishing.
He came because sinners needed saving.
The cross tells the truth about both realities at once:
Your sin is worse than your excuses want to admit.
And the mercy of Christ is greater than your shame wants you to believe.
Paul writes:
—1 Corinthians 6:18
Notice the verb.
φεύγετε — pheugete.
Flee.
Not negotiate.
Not investigate.
Not see how close you can stand to the fire while remaining technically innocent.
Flee.
Joseph understood this long before Paul wrote those words.
When Potiphar’s wife persistently pursued him and finally grabbed his garment, Joseph did not stay in the room to demonstrate how spiritually mature he was.
Genesis says he left the garment in her hand and fled.
Sometimes the most spiritual thing you can do is run.
Block the number.
Delete the conversation.
Leave the room.
Move the computer.
Install accountability.
Tell somebody trustworthy.
Stop meeting alone.
End the emotional affair before it becomes physical.
Stop calling pornography “stress relief.”
Stop feeding fantasies about somebody who does not belong to you.
Stop assuming secrecy means safety.
You do not prove your strength by remaining unnecessarily close to temptation.
You demonstrate wisdom by refusing to give temptation unnecessary access.
Jesus Himself taught His disciples to pray:
“Lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil.”
There is humility in that prayer.
Jesus did not train His followers to say:
“Father, make me so impressive that temptation becomes irrelevant.”
He taught dependence.
And dependence is where many gifted believers become vulnerable.
Calling can attract attention.
Attention can feed ego.
Ego can create entitlement.
Entitlement can whisper that normal boundaries are for ordinary people.
And then a gifted person begins believing that because God uses them publicly, God must approve of everything happening privately.
Never confuse usefulness with holiness.
God’s gifts are not certificates declaring that every area of your character is healthy.
Your platform cannot repent for you.
Your followers cannot sanctify you.
Your title cannot protect you.
Your theological knowledge cannot substitute for obedience.
Your anointing does not make you immune to sexual temptation.
You still need Jesus.
Every day.
Especially when nobody is watching.
Perhaps this is why Paul’s words in 1 Corinthians 9 are so sobering. He speaks about disciplining himself lest, after preaching to others, he himself should be disqualified.
Imagine that.
Paul took seriously the possibility of preaching truth to others while failing to govern himself faithfully.
That should destroy the mythology of spiritual celebrity.
There are no super-Christians.
There are only sheep who desperately need the Shepherd.
And some of the most dangerous seasons of your life may come immediately after spiritual victory.
After the conference.
After the breakthrough.
After the viral sermon.
After the answered prayer.
After somebody tells you how powerful your ministry is.
Because admiration can intoxicate the soul.
You begin believing the applause.
Then you begin protecting the image.
Then the image becomes more important than integrity.
And eventually you are maintaining two versions of yourself:
the person everybody sees...
and the person only God sees.
That divided life is exhausting.
Somebody reading this knows exactly what that exhaustion feels like.
You are tired of clearing your history.
Tired of hiding notifications.
Tired of changing passwords.
Tired of promising God you will stop.
Tired of worshiping on Sunday and collapsing privately on Monday.
Tired of wondering whether someone will discover what you have become.
Tired of hearing sermons about freedom while carrying chains underneath your church clothes.
Then stop running from the One who already knows.
Jesus is not waiting for you to surprise Him with your confession.
Bring it into the light.
John writes:
—1 John 1:9
The Greek verb translated “confess” is ὁμολογῶμεν — homologōmen, from homologeō—to confess, acknowledge, agree.
Biblical confession stops arguing with God about what God calls sin.
It agrees with Him.
No euphemisms.
No editing.
No excuses.
And then something extraordinary happens.
The sinner discovers that the throne he feared approaching is a throne of grace.
Not because sexual sin is insignificant.
Because Christ’s blood is sufficient.
Jesus carried shame to the cross.
Jesus bore judgment.
Jesus died for sinners.
Jesus rose victorious.
And therefore the Christian message to the sexually broken is neither:
“Your sin does not matter.”
Nor:
“You are permanently beyond redemption.”
The Gospel says:
Repent.
Come home.
There is mercy in Jesus Christ.
There is cleansing in Jesus Christ.
There is a new life in Jesus Christ.
There is power to say no in Jesus Christ.
There is restoration in Jesus Christ.
There is freedom that does not require pretending the battle never happened.
And if you have not fallen yet but recognize yourself standing dangerously close to the edge, do not wait for catastrophe to become humble.
You do not need a scandal before you establish boundaries.
You do not need an affair before you seek accountability.
You do not need your spouse crying across a table before you delete the secret relationship.
You do not need your children discovering pornography before you confess that you need help.
You do not need to lose everything before deciding Jesus is worth obeying.
Run now.
Not because you are terrified that God is waiting to crush you.
Run because sin wants something from you that it will never return.
Run because your marriage matters.
Run because your children matter.
Run because your conscience matters.
Run because the person you are secretly sexualizing bears the image of God and was never created to become an object for your appetite.
Run because your witness matters.
Run because holiness matters.
But above everything else...
run because Jesus is better.
Better than the screen.
Better than the fantasy.
Better than the forbidden conversation.
Better than the secret encounter.
Better than five minutes of pleasure followed by years of regret.
Christian purity cannot survive forever on fear alone.
Eventually your heart needs a greater affection.
Christ.
The One who knew every filthy chapter humanity would ever write and still stretched His arms across a cross.
The One who looked at sinners without becoming casual about sin.
The One who offered mercy without redefining righteousness.
The One who still says, in effect:
Come out of hiding.
Follow Me.
Maybe you already crossed the line.
Maybe your scandal already happened.
Maybe people know.
Maybe your marriage is wounded.
Maybe your reputation collapsed.
Maybe you are reading this thinking:
“This article came too late for me.”
No.
Not if you are still able to turn toward Christ.
David could not undo Uriah’s death.
Peter could not unsay his denials.
Paul could not resurrect the Christians whose persecution he had supported.
The Gospel does not give us a time machine.
It gives us something better.
A Redeemer.
Jesus does not rewrite everything by pretending the old pages never happened.
He rewrites everything by refusing to let sin have the final word over the repentant sinner.
That is From Scandal to Grace.
Not scandal to excuses.
Not scandal to image rehabilitation.
Not scandal to pretending consequences do not exist.
Scandal...
to repentance.
Repentance...
to mercy.
Mercy...
to transformation.
Transformation...
to a life that points people toward Jesus instead of toward the person you used to pretend to be.
And perhaps one day your greatest testimony will not be that you were never tempted.
Perhaps it will be that temptation exposed how desperately you needed Christ—and Christ taught you to walk in the light.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not owe strangers the details. But you can stop pretending.
Your honesty may become the permission somebody else needs to stop hiding too.

Invite your family, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelieving friends to follow too. Sometimes one piece of truth reaches someone at exactly the moment secrecy is about to become catastrophe.
Your support helps Gospel-centered content continue reaching people who may never walk into a church but will stop long enough to read something a friend shared.
And this is bigger than merchandise.
Guard your heart.
Flee what needs fleeing.
Confess what needs confessing.
Repair what needs repairing.
Bring trustworthy believers into battles you were never meant to fight secretly.
And stop believing that being used by God means you no longer need to desperately depend on God.
Your anointing will never make you immune to temptation.
But temptation does not have to become your master.
Sin does not have to write your ending.
Shame does not get the final sentence.
Jesus does.

And maybe that is the line you need to remember when the room is dark, the phone is glowing, nobody else would know, and temptation whispers that one secret decision cannot possibly change your story:
Before you trade your calling for a secret, remember—the Jesus who sees what nobody else sees is also the Jesus whose grace can give you the strength to walk away.
